metadata.title: Maximum Likelihood from Incomplete Data via the EM Algorithm
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available (pre-arXiv paper). Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Incomplete data setup
nodes.statement: Incomplete data: there exist sample spaces $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ with a many-to-one mapping $x \mapsto y(x)$; the observed $y \in \mathcal{Y}$ corresponds to an unobserved $x \in \mathcal{X}(y) = \{x : y(x)=y\}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Two sample spaces with a many-to-one map: only the image y is observed; x is the unobserved complete data.

nodes.name: Complete-data and incomplete-data densities
nodes.statement: $f(x \mid \phi)$ is the complete-data sampling density; the incomplete-data density satisfies $g(y \mid \phi) = \int_{\mathcal{X}(y)} f(x \mid \phi)\, dx$.
nodes.statement_clean: The observed-data density g is obtained by integrating the complete-data density f over the fibre X(y).

nodes.name: Conditional density of complete given incomplete data
nodes.statement: $k(x \mid y, \phi) = f(x \mid \phi) / g(y \mid \phi)$ is the conditional density of the complete data $x$ given the observed $y$ and parameter $\phi$.
nodes.statement_clean: Conditional density of x given y and phi, used as the basis for the E-step.

nodes.name: Regular exponential family complete-data model
nodes.statement: $f(x \mid \phi) = b(x)\, \exp(\phi\, t(x)^T) / a(\phi)$, where $\phi$ is a $1 \times r$ natural parameter restricted to a convex set $\Omega$ and $t(x)$ is the vector of complete-data sufficient statistics.
nodes.statement_clean: Standard regular exponential-family form for the complete-data sampling density.

nodes.name: Q-function (auxiliary objective)
nodes.statement: $Q(\phi' \mid \phi) = E[\log f(x \mid \phi') \mid y, \phi]$, the conditional expectation of the complete-data log-likelihood at $\phi'$ given the observed $y$ and current parameter $\phi$.
nodes.statement_clean: Q is the expected complete-data log-likelihood; the EM algorithm maximizes it in the M-step.

nodes.name: H-function
nodes.statement: $H(\phi' \mid \phi) = E[\log k(x \mid y, \phi') \mid y, \phi]$, so that the observed log-likelihood decomposes as $L(\phi') = Q(\phi' \mid \phi) - H(\phi' \mid \phi)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Decomposition L = Q - H linking observed log-likelihood to the auxiliary functions.

nodes.name: Generalized EM (GEM) algorithm
nodes.statement: An iterative algorithm with mapping $M : \Omega \to \Omega$ is a GEM algorithm if $Q(M(\phi) \mid \phi) \geq Q(\phi \mid \phi)$ for every $\phi \in \Omega$.
nodes.statement_clean: GEM is any iteration whose mapping increases (or maintains) the Q-function at each step.

nodes.name: EM Algorithm (regular exponential family form)
nodes.statement: Iterative algorithm alternating an E-step (compute conditional expectation of sufficient statistics) and an M-step (solve the complete-data likelihood equations) to find a maximizer of $L(\phi) = \log g(y \mid \phi)$.
output: Sequence $\phi^{(p)}$ converging (under conditions) to a maximizer $\phi^*$ of the observed log-likelihood $L(\phi)$
nodes.pseudocode: Repeat for p = 0,1,2,...: E-step: compute t^{(p)} = E[t(x) | y, phi^{(p)}]. M-step: choose phi^{(p+1)} as the solution of E[t(x) | phi] = t^{(p)}.

nodes.name: E-step (exponential family)
nodes.statement: Estimate the complete-data sufficient statistics by $t^{(p)} = E[t(x) \mid y, \phi^{(p)}]$.

nodes.name: M-step (exponential family)
nodes.statement: Determine $\phi^{(p+1)}$ as the solution of the likelihood equations $E[t(x) \mid \phi] = t^{(p)}$.

nodes.name: Iterate until convergence
nodes.statement: Repeat the E- and M-steps; under regularity conditions (Theorems 1-4) the sequence $\phi^{(p)}$ converges to a stationary point $\phi^*$ of $L(\phi)$.

nodes.name: EM Algorithm (general form)
nodes.statement: General iteration: E-step computes $Q(\phi \mid \phi^{(p)}) = E[\log f(x \mid \phi) \mid y, \phi^{(p)}]$; M-step chooses $\phi^{(p+1)} \in \Omega$ maximizing $Q(\phi \mid \phi^{(p)})$.
nodes.pseudocode: Repeat: E-step compute Q(phi | phi^{(p)}); M-step choose phi^{(p+1)} maximizing Q(. | phi^{(p)}).

nodes.name: E-step (general)
nodes.statement: Compute the auxiliary function $Q(\phi \mid \phi^{(p)}) = E[\log f(x \mid \phi) \mid y, \phi^{(p)}]$.

nodes.name: M-step (general)
nodes.statement: Choose $\phi^{(p+1)}$ to be a value of $\phi \in \Omega$ that maximizes $Q(\phi \mid \phi^{(p)})$.

nodes.name: EM Algorithm for Posterior Mode
nodes.statement: Bayesian variant: at the M-step maximize $Q(\phi \mid \phi^{(p)}) + G(\phi)$, where $G(\phi)$ is the log of the prior density of $\phi$.
output: Sequence converging to the posterior mode of $\phi$
nodes.pseudocode: Same E-step as AP200.2; M-step maximizes Q(phi | phi^{(p)}) + G(phi).

nodes.name: Score-function representation
nodes.statement: $DL(\phi) = -E[t \mid \phi] + E[t \mid y, \phi]$, so the gradient of the observed log-likelihood is the difference of conditional and unconditional expectations of the sufficient statistics.
nodes.statement_clean: Sundberg / Martin-Lof formula: gradient of L equals the difference of conditional and unconditional expected sufficient statistics.

nodes.name: Sundberg cumulant formula
nodes.statement: $D^k L(\phi) = -K_k(t \mid \phi) + K_k(t \mid y, \phi)$; the $k$-th derivative of the log-likelihood is the difference of the $k$-th cumulants of the sufficient statistics.
nodes.statement_clean: Higher-derivative analogue: D^k L = (conditional - unconditional) k-th cumulants of t.

nodes.name: Identity L = Q - H
nodes.statement: $L(\phi') = Q(\phi' \mid \phi) - H(\phi' \mid \phi)$ for all $(\phi', \phi) \in \Omega \times \Omega$.
nodes.statement_clean: Decomposition of the observed log-likelihood used to prove monotone increase.

nodes.name: Lemma 1 (Jensen inequality for H)
nodes.statement: For any $(\phi', \phi) \in \Omega \times \Omega$, $H(\phi' \mid \phi) \leq H(\phi \mid \phi)$, with equality iff $k(x \mid y, \phi') = k(x \mid y, \phi)$ almost everywhere.
conclusions: Equality iff $k(x \mid y, \phi') = k(x \mid y, \phi)$ a.e.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Standard consequence of Jensen's inequality applied to the conditional density $k(x \mid y, \phi)$; see formulae (1e.5.6) and (1e.6.6) of Rao (1965).

nodes.name: Theorem 1 (Monotone increase of likelihood for GEM)
nodes.statement: For every GEM algorithm, $L(M(\phi)) \geq L(\phi)$ for all $\phi \in \Omega$, with equality iff $Q(M(\phi) \mid \phi) = Q(\phi \mid \phi)$ and $k(x \mid y, M(\phi)) = k(x \mid y, \phi)$ almost everywhere.
assumptions: The mapping $M$ defines a GEM algorithm: $Q(M(\phi) \mid \phi) \geq Q(\phi \mid \phi)$ for all $\phi$
conclusions: Equality holds iff $Q(M(\phi)\mid\phi) = Q(\phi\mid\phi)$ and $k(x\mid y, M(\phi)) = k(x\mid y, \phi)$ a.e.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Write $L(M(\phi)) - L(\phi) = [Q(M(\phi)\mid\phi) - Q(\phi\mid\phi)] + [H(\phi\mid\phi) - H(M(\phi)\mid\phi)]$; the first bracket is $\geq 0$ by GEM, the second is $\geq 0$ by Lemma 1.

nodes.name: Corollary 1 (MLE is fixed point of GEM)
nodes.statement: If $\phi^* \in \Omega$ satisfies $L(\phi^*) \geq L(\phi)$ for all $\phi \in \Omega$, then for every GEM algorithm $L(M(\phi^*)) = L(\phi^*)$, $Q(M(\phi^*)\mid\phi^*) = Q(\phi^*\mid\phi^*)$, and $k(x\mid y, M(\phi^*)) = k(x\mid y, \phi^*)$ a.e.

nodes.name: Corollary 2 (Strict global max is fixed point)
nodes.statement: If $L(\phi^*) > L(\phi)$ for all $\phi \neq \phi^*$ in $\Omega$, then $M(\phi^*) = \phi^*$ for every GEM algorithm.
assumptions: $\phi^*$ is a strict global maximum of $L$

nodes.name: Theorem 2 (Convergence of GEM iterates)
nodes.statement: Suppose $\phi^{(p)}$ is a GEM sequence such that (1) $L(\phi^{(p)})$ is bounded and (2) $Q(\phi^{(p+1)}\mid\phi^{(p)}) - Q(\phi^{(p)}\mid\phi^{(p)}) \geq \lambda (\phi^{(p+1)} - \phi^{(p)})(\phi^{(p+1)} - \phi^{(p)})^T$ for some scalar $\lambda > 0$. Then $\phi^{(p)}$ converges to some $\phi^*$ in the closure of $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Use boundedness of $L(\phi^{(p)})$ and Theorem 1 to get a Cauchy summability bound on the $Q$ increments; combine with assumption (2) to bound $\|\phi^{(p+r)}-\phi^{(p)}\|$ by $\sqrt{\epsilon/\lambda}$, giving Cauchy convergence.

nodes.name: Bound Q-increments via L convergence
nodes.statement: Boundedness of $L(\phi^{(p)})$ and monotonicity (Theorem 1) imply $\sum_{j=1}^{r} \{Q(\phi^{(p+j)}\mid\phi^{(p+j-1)}) - Q(\phi^{(p+j-1)}\mid\phi^{(p+j-1)})\} < \epsilon$ for all $p \geq p(\epsilon)$.

nodes.name: Apply quadratic lower bound and conclude Cauchy
nodes.statement: Apply assumption (2) to each $Q$-increment and sum: $\lambda \sum_{j=1}^r \| \phi^{(p+j)}-\phi^{(p+j-1)} \|^2 < \epsilon$, hence $\| \phi^{(p+r)} - \phi^{(p)} \| \leq \sqrt{\epsilon/\lambda}$, proving Cauchy convergence to $\phi^*$.

nodes.name: Lemma 2 (score-function identities)
nodes.statement: For all $\phi \in \Omega$: $D^{10} H(\phi \mid \phi) = 0$ and $-D^{20} H(\phi \mid \phi) = V[D^{10} \log k(x\mid y, \phi) \mid y, \phi]$ (the conditional Fisher information for the missing data).
assumptions: Sufficient regularity to differentiate under the integral
conclusions: $-D^{20} H(\phi \mid \phi)$ equals the conditional Fisher information of $k(x\mid y, \phi)$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Differentiate $\int k(x\mid y, \phi') dx = 1$ once and twice under the integral sign and evaluate at $\phi' = \phi$, yielding the score and information identities.

nodes.name: Theorem 3 (Convergence under negative-definite Q)
nodes.statement: If $\phi^{(p)}$ is a GEM sequence with $D^{10} Q(\phi^{(p+1)}\mid\phi^{(p)}) = 0$, then there exists $\phi^*_{(p+1)}$ on the segment $[\phi^{(p)}, \phi^{(p+1)}]$ with a Taylor identity; if further $D^{20} Q(\phi^*_{(p+1)}\mid\phi^{(p)})$ is negative definite with eigenvalues bounded away from zero and $L(\phi^{(p)})$ is bounded, the sequence converges to some $\phi^*$ in $\overline{\Omega}$.
assumptions: $D^{20} Q(\phi^*_{(p+1)}\mid\phi^{(p)})$ is negative definite, eigenvalues bounded away from zero
conclusions: There exists $\phi^*_{(p+1)}$ on the segment $[\phi^{(p)}, \phi^{(p+1)}]$ giving a Taylor remainder identity

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Expand $Q(\phi\mid\phi^{(p)})$ in Taylor series about $\phi^{(p+1)}$, evaluate at $\phi = \phi^{(p)}$ using $D^{10}Q(\phi^{(p+1)}\mid\phi^{(p)}) = 0$; the remainder gives the quadratic lower bound (assumption (2) of Theorem 2), so Theorem 2 applies.

nodes.name: Theorem 4 (Rate of convergence at fixed point)
nodes.statement: Suppose $\phi^{(p)}$ converges to $\phi^*$, $D^{10} Q(\phi^{(p+1)}\mid\phi^{(p)}) = 0$, and $D^{20} Q(\phi^{(p+1)}\mid\phi^{(p)})$ is negative definite with eigenvalues bounded away from zero. Then $D^{10} L(\phi^*) = 0$, $D^{20} Q(\phi^*\mid\phi^*)$ is negative definite, and $DM(\phi^*) = D^{20} H(\phi^*\mid\phi^*) [D^{20} Q(\phi^*\mid\phi^*)]^{-1}$.
assumptions: $D^{20} Q(\phi^{(p+1)}\mid\phi^{(p)})$ negative definite, eigenvalues bounded away from zero
conclusions: $D^{10} L(\phi^*) = 0$ (limit point is a stationary point of $L$)
$DM(\phi^*) = D^{20} H(\phi^*\mid\phi^*) [D^{20} Q(\phi^*\mid\phi^*)]^{-1}$ (rate of convergence matrix)

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: Use $D^{10} L = D^{10} Q - D^{10} H$; the second term vanishes by Lemma 2, the first by the M-step assumption. For the rate matrix, expand $M(\phi^{(p)}) - M(\phi^*)$ in Taylor series and use $D^{10} Q(M(\phi^*)\mid\phi^*) = 0$.

nodes.name: Limit of score equation gives DL = 0
nodes.statement: From $D^{10} L(\phi) = D^{10} Q(\phi\mid\phi) - D^{10} H(\phi\mid\phi)$, the second term is $0$ by Lemma 2; the first vanishes in the limit by assumption (2). Hence $D^{10} L(\phi^*) = 0$.

nodes.name: Negative definiteness of $D^{20} Q(\phi^*\mid\phi^*)$
nodes.statement: $D^{20} Q(\phi^*\mid\phi^*)$ is the limit of $D^{20} Q(\phi^{(p+1)}\mid\phi^{(p)})$, whose eigenvalues are bounded away from zero, so the limit is negative definite.

nodes.name: Derive rate matrix $DM(\phi^*)$
nodes.statement: Expand $D^{10} Q(M(\phi)\mid\phi)$ around $\phi^*$ and use $M(\phi^*) = \phi^*$ to obtain $DM(\phi^*) = D^{20} H(\phi^*\mid\phi^*)[D^{20} Q(\phi^*\mid\phi^*)]^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Geometric rate of convergence
nodes.statement: When the eigenvalues of $DM(\phi^*)$ all lie in $[0,1)$, the largest eigenvalue gives the (linear) rate of convergence of the EM algorithm; small information loss due to incompleteness yields fast convergence.

nodes.name: Saddle points and ridges
nodes.statement: If $DM(\phi^*)$ has eigenvalues $> 1$, $\phi^*$ may be a saddle of $L$; an eigenvalue equal to $1$ in a neighbourhood implies a ridge of local maxima in $L$ through $\phi^*$.

nodes.name: Acceleration possibilities
nodes.statement: Convergence may be accelerated by Newton-type steps using second derivatives, by Aitken's $\Delta^2$ process when $\phi$ is scalar, or by exploiting factorized likelihoods (Rubin 1974) so that EM is applied to less-incomplete sub-likelihoods.

nodes.name: Multinomial genetic model (Rao 1965)
nodes.statement: $n=197$ animals are distributed multinomially among 4 categories with cell probabilities $(\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{4}\pi, \tfrac{1}{4}(1-\pi), \tfrac{1}{4}(1-\pi), \tfrac{1}{4}\pi)$; the EM algorithm splits the first cell into two ($\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $\tfrac{1}{4}\pi$) so the complete data are 5-category multinomial. Starting from $\pi^{(0)} = 0.5$ the algorithm converges in 8 iterations to $\pi^*$ with empirical rate $\approx 0.1328$.

nodes.name: Multinomial sampling with missing cells (Section 4.1.1)
nodes.statement: Discrete population sampling where some observations are reported only as belonging to aggregates of cells; the E-step assigns fractional indicators to the missing cells, the M-step is ordinary multinomial MLE on observed plus assigned counts (Hartley 1958).

nodes.name: Normal linear model with missing data (Section 4.1.2)
nodes.statement: Least-squares estimation in ANOVA / normal linear models with missing data (Healy & Westmacott 1956): E-step fills missing values with their conditional means, M-step refits least squares; iterates to MLE.

nodes.name: Multivariate normal sampling (Section 4.1.3)
nodes.statement: Different individuals observed on different subsets of $p$ variables: E-step computes conditional means, mean squares, and mean products of missing values; M-step takes these as if observed and produces standard mean/covariance MLEs (Orchard & Woodbury 1972; Beale & Little 1975).

nodes.name: Grouping, censoring and truncation (Section 4.2)
nodes.statement: Sample space $\mathcal{Z}$ partitioned into $\mathcal{Z}_0,\dots,\mathcal{Z}_t$; only $z_{0j}$ values, counts $n_1,\dots,n_{t-1}$ in grouping/censoring regions, and no count in truncation region $\mathcal{Z}_t$ are observed. The EM algorithm augments with negative-binomial-distributed truncated points so the complete-data MLE has closed form.

nodes.name: Probit model of quantal assay
nodes.statement: Animal lives ($y=0$) or dies ($y=1$) according to whether unobserved tolerance $z \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ exceeds presented stimulus $S_i$; EM treats the tolerance as censored data and recovers $\mu, \sigma^2$ (Mantel & Greenhouse 1967).

nodes.name: Finite mixtures (Section 4.3)
nodes.statement: Observations $y_i$ each associated with an unobserved indicator $z_i \in \{e_1,\dots,e_R\}$ of the latent state; EM E-step computes posterior class probabilities and M-step performs weighted complete-data MLE (Hasselblad 1966, 1969; Day 1969; Wolfe 1970; Baum et al. 1970 for HMMs).

nodes.name: Variance components / mixed model (Section 4.4)
nodes.statement: $y = A x$ with $x_i \sim N(0, \sigma_i^2 I)$ independent; the incomplete-data covariance is $\Sigma = \sum_i \sigma_i^2 Z_i$ with $Z_i = A_i A_i^T$. EM treats $x$ as missing: E-step computes $E[x_i^T x_i \mid y, \sigma^{2(p)}]$, M-step sets $\sigma_i^{2(p+1)} = E[x_i^T x_i]/r_i$.

nodes.name: Hyperparameter estimation / empirical Bayes (Section 4.5)
nodes.statement: Hierarchical model with $y \sim l(y\mid\theta)$ and $\theta \sim h(\theta\mid\phi)$ where $\phi$ are hyperparameters; EM applied with $x = (y,\theta)$ yields the marginal MLE of $\phi$ from $g(y\mid\phi) = \int l(y\mid\theta) h(\theta\mid\phi) d\theta$.

nodes.name: Iteratively reweighted least squares (Section 4.6)
nodes.statement: $y_i \mid q_i \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2/q_i)$ with $q_i$ unobserved from $h(q_i)$; the EM algorithm reduces to iteratively reweighted least squares with weights $w_i = E[q_i \mid y_i, \mu^{(p)}, \sigma^{2(p)}]$. For $h$ of $\chi^2_r$ form $y_i$ has a $t_r$ distribution; for mixture-of-normals $h$ one obtains contaminated-normal estimation.

nodes.name: Factor analysis (Section 4.7)
nodes.statement: Observed $y$ ($n\times p$) with unobserved factor scores $z$ ($n\times q$, $q<p$); model $y_i \mid z_i \sim N(\alpha + \beta z_i, \tau^2)$ with $z_i \sim N(0, R)$. EM alternates back-and-forth least-squares calculations on the augmented cross-product matrix to estimate factor loadings $\beta$ and uniquenesses $\tau^2$.

nodes.name: Maximum likelihood from incomplete data
nodes.statement: Given observed data $y$ with sampling density $g(y\mid\phi) = \int_{\mathcal{X}(y)} f(x\mid\phi)\, dx$, find $\phi^* = \arg\max_{\phi\in\Omega} L(\phi)$ where $L(\phi) = \log g(y\mid\phi)$.
